headline: Price Tags, Crowded Orbits and Burning Peat
teaser: Do record holiday sales mean families are better off? Should one country decide how a million satellites fill the sky? And can orangutans survive when their forests go up in smoke?

articles.title: Black Friday on a Budget: Bigger Sales, Tighter Wallets
articles.dek: US holiday sales are forecast to pass $1 trillion for the first time. Is that a sign of a strong economy, or of how expensive ordinary life has become?
paras: Every year, the day after Thanksgiving marks the unofficial start of the American holiday shopping season. Stores open early, websites flash countdown timers, and news reports track how much money people spend. This year's Black Friday, which fell on November 27, arrived with impressive headline numbers. Behind them, however, lies a more complicated story about prices, pressure and who is really doing the spending.

On paper, the forecasts look strong. The National Retail Federation (NRF), the industry's largest trade group, expects retail sales in November and December to rise by 4.2 percent compared with last year, pushing the total to just above $1 trillion for the first time. Other forecasters are even more optimistic: the Mastercard Economics Institute and the consultancy EY-Parthenon each predict growth of more than 5 percent. A survey by Deloitte found that 87 percent of shoppers planned to buy something during the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday, the highest share in a decade.

Yet economists warn that a bigger number does not always mean a bigger shopping basket. Sales are measured in dollars, and dollars buy less when prices rise. According to Reuters, inflation is running at about 3.8 percent, roughly a point higher than in each of the previous two years. If prices are climbing by nearly 4 percent, then most of a 4.2 percent rise in sales simply reflects higher price tags rather than more goods leaving the shelves. Economists call this the difference between nominal growth, measured in money, and real growth, measured in actual quantities. Tom Fullerton, an economist at the University of Texas at El Paso, put it plainly: spending is growing largely "because prices are higher."

Some of those higher prices are linked to tariffs, the taxes a government places on imported goods. Retailers that import toys, electronics and clothing have passed part of the extra cost on to customers, and toy prices alone have risen by 13.2 percent since the start of the year. Not every increase, however, can be blamed on trade policy. A Canadian retail consultant, Kyle Peacock, has accused some sellers of "tariff gouging," raising prices even on products that face no new tariff and using the headlines as cover. Shoppers, he argues, should compare prices carefully rather than assume every rise is unavoidable.

Consumers are clearly adapting. In an NRF survey this month, 82 percent of shoppers said they were taking steps to manage holiday costs, such as buying cheaper gifts or switching to lesser-known brands. Many are also spreading their purchases over a longer period. Only 17 percent now plan to concentrate their shopping around Black Friday itself, down from 25 percent a year ago, and the busiest weeks are shifting toward early and mid-December. Retailers, for their part, are running longer promotions with smaller discounts, which means the single dramatic "doorbuster" deal is becoming rarer.

Optimists still see reasons for confidence. "People like to spend during the holidays," said Katie Thomas of the Kearney Consumer Institute, and the record share of people planning to shop suggests that demand has not collapsed. From this perspective, the American consumer remains remarkably resilient, continuing to spend despite years of rising costs. Healthy holiday sales also support millions of jobs in stores, warehouses and delivery services, so a strong season matters well beyond the shopping mall.

Pessimists, by contrast, point to signs of strain beneath the surface. Kearney's own research shows that middle- and lower-income households are more likely to cut back, while the head of the department store chain Kohl's has described an "increasingly choiceful" customer looking to stretch every dollar. Analysts at the bank UBS have added a further warning: a recent fall in stock prices could make even wealthier shoppers, whose spending has propped up the economy, more cautious. If growth depends mainly on the richest households, the overall figures may hide real hardship for everyone else.

Both sides agree on one point: the headline number alone cannot tell us how families are really doing. A trillion-dollar season sounds like a celebration, but it may also be a sign of how expensive ordinary life has become. For students of economics, Black Friday offers a useful lesson. Before celebrating or worrying about any statistic, it is worth asking what is being measured, whose behaviour it reflects, and what it leaves out.

words.def: able to keep going or recover quickly after difficulties

keySentences.text: Behind them, however, lies a more complicated story about prices, pressure and who is really doing the spending.
keySentences.note: The sentence after “however” sets up the whole article: the big numbers hide a more complex reality. TOEFL main-idea answers often follow a contrast word.

keySentences.text: If prices are climbing by nearly 4 percent, then most of a 4.2 percent rise in sales simply reflects higher price tags rather than more goods leaving the shelves.
keySentences.note: This “if … then” sentence explains the key economic idea of the passage: rising prices, not more goods, drive most of the growth.

keySentences.text: Not every increase, however, can be blamed on trade policy.
keySentences.note: A short sentence that turns the paragraph from tariffs to “tariff gouging.” Rhetorical-purpose questions often ask why an example follows such a turn.

keySentences.text: From this perspective, the American consumer remains remarkably resilient, continuing to spend despite years of rising costs.
keySentences.note: “From this perspective” signals one side's view, not the author's. Inference questions test whether you can tell whose opinion is being reported.

keySentences.text: If growth depends mainly on the richest households, the overall figures may hide real hardship for everyone else.
keySentences.note: “May hide” is cautious language. Answers with “proves” or “always” would be too extreme for this claim.

keySentences.text: Before celebrating or worrying about any statistic, it is worth asking what is being measured, whose behaviour it reflects, and what it leaves out.
keySentences.note: The final sentence gives the author's lesson. It is a strong candidate for a summary's main idea.

questions.why: The phrase that follows, “continuing to spend despite years of rising costs,” defines “resilient”: consumers keep going even under pressure.
optWhy: Correct. “Resilient, continuing to spend despite years of rising costs” = able to keep going despite difficulties.
Wrong: another meaning of the word. Materials such as rubber are “resilient” when they spring back into shape, but the text describes people who keep spending, not a physical object.
Wrong: meaning distorted. The text praises consumers for carrying on “despite years of rising costs”; it does not say they refuse to change. In fact paragraph 5 says “Consumers are clearly adapting.”
Wrong: opposite idea. Being careful with money is what the pessimists describe in paragraph 7 (“stretch every dollar”); “resilient” here means consumers keep spending.

Wrong: too extreme. The text says “most of” the rise reflects higher prices, not all of it, and never says real sales will fall.
Wrong: reversed. “Sales are measured in dollars,” not in actual quantities; counting items would be real growth.
Correct. “Most of a 4.2 percent rise … reflects higher price tags” → only a small part reflects more goods, so the real increase is small.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 7? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.
opts: UBS analysts say wealthy shoppers caused the recent fall in stock prices.
UBS analysts also warn that falling share prices may lead even the wealthier shoppers who have supported the economy to spend more carefully.
UBS analysts believe wealthy shoppers will keep the economy strong despite the fall in share prices.

questions.evidence: a recent fall in stock prices could make even wealthier shoppers, whose spending has propped up the economy, more cautious
questions.why: The sentence says a fall in stock prices could make wealthier shoppers, who have supported the economy, more cautious. Option B keeps all three parts and the cautious “could/may.”
optWhy: Wrong: cause reversed. In the sentence, the fall in stock prices affects shoppers; shoppers did not cause the fall.
Correct. “could make even wealthier shoppers … more cautious” = may lead even wealthier shoppers to spend more carefully; “propped up the economy” = supported the economy.
Wrong: contradiction. The sentence is a “warning” that these shoppers may become cautious, not a prediction that they will keep the economy strong.
Wrong: too certain. The sentence uses “could” about the future; it does not say the economy has “already” declined.

ctx.text: Analysts at the bank UBS have added a further warning: a recent fall in stock prices could make even wealthier shoppers, whose spending has propped up the economy, more cautious.

“Could” is a possibility, so the right answer must also be cautious (may).

speak.p: Some people think big shopping events like Black Friday are good because they help families save money and support jobs. Others think they mainly encourage people to buy things they do not need. Which view do you agree with? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: Pick one side; give two reasons (saving money, jobs, waste, pressure to buy); add a personal or class example; end with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Lin: This year, US holiday sales are expected to pass $1 trillion for the first time. However, with inflation near 4 percent, most of that growth reflects higher prices rather than more goods. Some people think record sales show the economy is healthy. Others believe headline numbers like this hide how hard life is for many families. Which view do you find more convincing, and why?
Amy: “I think record sales are good news. If people were really struggling, they would not plan to shop in such large numbers. Strong spending also keeps millions of workers in stores and warehouses employed.”
Kevin: “I'm not convinced. If prices are rising almost as fast as sales, people are paying more for the same things. And if mainly wealthy families are spending, the total hides the pressure on everyone else.”
steps: State clearly whether record sales mean a healthy economy.
Respond to Amy or Kevin and add a new reason.
Use a fact from the article (4.2 percent vs 3.8 percent, 82 percent cutting costs).

articles.title: A Million Satellites for AI: Progress in Orbit or a Crowded Sky?
articles.dek: US regulators have cleared SpaceX to launch up to a million computing satellites. Is this a smart answer to AI's hunger for energy, or a risky race to claim a shared space?
paras: For most of the space age, satellites were rare and expensive objects, launched one or two at a time. That era is ending. On November 25, the United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) gave SpaceX permission to place up to one million satellites in orbit around Earth. The satellites would not carry television signals or internet traffic for homes. Instead, they would form "Starmind," a network of orbiting computers designed to run artificial intelligence.

The idea behind Starmind is simple, even if building it will not be. Training and running AI systems requires enormous data centres, which consume vast amounts of electricity, need water for cooling and occupy large areas of land. In orbit, a satellite can collect solar energy almost continuously, without clouds or night-time interruptions, and release excess heat into space through radiators. According to the trade publication Via Satellite, each Starmind satellite would carry a computing payload using about 175 kilowatts of power on average. Supporters argue that moving computing off the planet could ease the pressure that AI is placing on power grids and local communities.

The approval comes with detailed conditions. The satellites must fly in six orbital "shells" between 500 and 1,002 kilometres above Earth, and they will communicate mainly by laser links rather than radio. SpaceX must have its first satellite operating by 2033, reach 100,000 satellites by 2035 and complete the full constellation by 2040, or the licence will lapse. Crucially, the FCC found that SpaceX's plan for avoiding space debris met its rules only for satellites below 600 kilometres. Since four of the six shells sit above that height, the company must submit a final debris plan before it can use them.

Those conditions reflect a concern that worries many scientists: orbital debris. Objects in low orbit travel at around 28,000 kilometres per hour, so even a fragment the size of a coin can destroy a satellite. Experts have long warned of the Kessler syndrome, a chain reaction in which collisions create debris that causes further collisions, until some orbits become too dangerous to use. Today, the total number of active satellites is in the tens of thousands at most. Adding a million more, critics say, would transform the orbital environment in ways no one can fully predict.

Astronomers have a separate complaint. Bright satellites leave streaks across telescope images, and a sky filled with sunlit machines could interfere with research and change the view of the night sky for everyone. The American Astronomical Society said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision. The FCC, however, ruled that the brightness of satellites falls outside the scope of a licence that regulates radio signals. The Secure World Foundation, a group focused on the sustainable use of space, has argued that projects on this scale should be approved in phases, with each stage depending on proof that the previous one works safely.

Competitors raised doubts of a different kind. Amazon, which is building its own satellite network, called SpaceX's proposal "a lofty ambition rather than a real plan," and the satellite company Viasat also asked regulators to reject it. The FCC replied that questions about whether a business will succeed are not part of its job, and it declined to block the application. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr praised the project for moving computing capacity beyond Earth, while Elon Musk, SpaceX's founder, predicted it would be "a great asset to America and the world." Other firms, including Blue Origin and the start-up Starcloud, have filed plans for tens of thousands of orbital computers of their own.

Behind the technical arguments lies a larger question about who controls space. Low Earth orbit is not owned by any one country, yet decisions made by a single national regulator can shape it for everyone. Supporters see the FCC's approval as a bold step that keeps innovation moving and may reduce AI's environmental footprint on the ground. Critics see a race to claim a shared resource before the rules are ready. The million-satellite figure is a ceiling, not a guarantee, and the engineering and economics remain unproven. Even so, the decision marks the moment when the idea of an industrial orbit, crowded with working machines, moved from science fiction to official paperwork.

keySentences.text: Instead, they would form "Starmind," a network of orbiting computers designed to run artificial intelligence.
keySentences.note: “Instead” corrects a likely assumption (internet satellites) and names the real purpose. Contrast words often introduce the main idea.

keySentences.text: Supporters argue that moving computing off the planet could ease the pressure that AI is placing on power grids and local communities.
keySentences.note: This sentence gives the supporters' reason for the project. Notice “argue” and “could”: it is a claim, not a proven fact.

keySentences.text: Crucially, the FCC found that SpaceX's plan for avoiding space debris met its rules only for satellites below 600 kilometres.
keySentences.note: “Crucially” marks the most important condition. Detail questions often test limiting words such as “only.”

keySentences.text: Adding a million more, critics say, would transform the orbital environment in ways no one can fully predict.
keySentences.note: The critics' main worry is uncertainty. Compare “tens of thousands” today with “a million more” to see the scale.

keySentences.text: The FCC replied that questions about whether a business will succeed are not part of its job, and it declined to block the application.
keySentences.note: This explains how the regulator answered business objections. Sentence-simplification questions test whether you keep both the reason and the result.

keySentences.text: Critics see a race to claim a shared resource before the rules are ready.
keySentences.note: A short sentence that sums up the opposing view. It links to the larger question of who controls space.

articles.title: Smoke over Borneo: What Wildfires Mean for Orangutans
articles.dek: Indonesia's worst fire season in a decade has reached the forests where orangutans live. Is this a natural disaster, or the result of human choices about land?

sources.name: Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior via EurekAlert, 3 Nov 2026

paras: Orangutans spend almost their entire lives in the treetops of the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, moving slowly from branch to branch in search of fruit. These great apes share about 97 percent of their DNA with humans and are known for their intelligence and gentle nature. This year, however, their forest home has been burning. A strong El Niño, a climate pattern that brings unusually dry weather to Indonesia, has fuelled one of the worst wildfire seasons in more than a decade, and scientists fear the damage to orangutans may last for years.

The scale of the fires is hard to measure, and estimates vary widely. Indonesia's government reported that more than 202,000 hectares burned between January and July, while the independent monitoring group Nusantara Atlas estimated about 900,000 hectares by the end of August. Whatever the exact figure, the fires have struck the places where orangutans live. According to the conservation network IUCN, blazes have affected habitats holding 52 percent of Borneo's orangutans, including 13 of the 20 largest populations. The Bornean orangutan is already classed as Critically Endangered, one step away from extinction in the wild.

Many of the fires are burning in peatland, a type of wetland where dead plant material has built up over thousands of years. When it is wet, peat rarely burns. When it is drained to make way for plantations, it dries out and can smoulder underground for weeks, releasing thick smoke and huge amounts of carbon. In September, Indonesia's forestry ministry froze the business permit of one pulpwood company, Mayawana, whose concession includes large areas of peat and where fires had spread across cleared land. For this reason, many researchers argue that the disaster is not only natural but also the result of human decisions about land.

Long-term research suggests that the harm to orangutans continues long after the smoke clears. At the Tuanan research station in Central Kalimantan, scientists from the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior have followed the same orangutans since 2003. After severe fires in 2015, smoke covered the area for three months, and fruit production fell sharply for about two and a half years. During that period, researchers recorded no pregnancies among the females they studied, and three of the oldest females had disappeared by late 2017. The researchers caution that they cannot prove the fires caused these losses, but the pattern is troubling.

The timing matters because orangutans reproduce extremely slowly. A female usually gives birth only once every six to eight years, so a population that loses even a few adult females may need decades to recover. This year's fires have destroyed an estimated 30 percent of the Tuanan study area, compared with about 15 percent of the forest in 2015. "I'm afraid that the toll will be worse than last time," said Maria van Noordwijk, a researcher who has worked at the site for many years.

Not everyone agrees on where attention should go first. Rescue groups have saved dozens of injured or stranded orangutans this season, and many people see emergency action as the most urgent priority. "Years of successful conservation work can be undone incredibly quickly by a major fire," warned Gavin Bruce of the charity International Animal Rescue. Others argue that rescues alone cannot solve the problem. The Forum Orangutan Indonesia has called for rewetting peatlands and stopping drainage and deforestation, insisting that emergency response must be followed by long-term investment in prevention.

There is also debate about how much blame to place on climate and how much on land use. El Niño events are natural, but a warming climate may make them more extreme, while drained peat and cleared forest turn dry seasons into disasters. Economic development brings jobs and income to Indonesian communities, which makes the choices difficult. What is clear is that the future of the orangutan depends less on any single rescue than on whether the forests and peatlands it needs can be kept wet, connected and standing.

parts.task: Read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
parts.text: This year, American retailers are hoping that Black Friday will {1} up to its reputation as the busiest shopping day of the year. Forecasters expect holiday sales to pass $1 trillion, but economists warn that the figure should be taken with a {2} of salt. With inflation running at nearly 4 percent, higher prices {3} for most of the increase. Many families are feeling the {4} and have started to cut back on gifts. Others are trying to make their money go {5} by switching to cheaper brands. Retailers, meanwhile, are offering longer promotions, but the discounts are smaller than shoppers have come to {6}. items.why: “Live up to” a reputation means to be as good as people expect. The other verbs do not form this phrase.

“Account for” means to form or explain a part of something; only “account” takes “for” here.
“Feel the pinch” means to have less money than before. The other nouns do not form this idiom.
We say “make your money go further,” meaning to buy more with the same amount.
“Have come to expect” describes something people now regard as normal. “Hope,” “wish” and “want” do not fit the idea of a habit formed over time.
“Warn that + clause” reports a caution. “Alert,” “notify” and “advise” normally need an object (alert someone).
We say “cast light on” or “shed light on,” meaning to help explain something.

Critics, however, are worried {12} the risk of collisions. They point out that a fragment no bigger {13} a coin can destroy a satellite. Not {14} have astronomers objected, but rival companies have also questioned whether the project is realistic. The regulator replied that judging a company's chances of success is not its job, {15} is why it refused to block the plan. Even so, the company must meet strict deadlines, {16} it will lose its licence.

items.why: A quantifier such as “each” or “all” before “of which” refers back to the satellites.
“Unlike” introduces a contrast between satellites and data centres on Earth.
“If the plan succeeds” sets a condition for the result in the main clause.
The adjective “worried” is followed by “about.”
“No bigger than” is a comparative structure, so “than” is needed.
“Not only … but also” with inversion: “Not only have astronomers objected.”
“Which” refers back to the whole previous clause (that judging success is not its job).
“Or” / “otherwise” introduces the result if the deadlines are not met.

parts.title: Word formation
parts.task: Use the word given in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
parts.text: This year's fires in Indonesia were made worse by {17} dry weather linked to El Niño. Many blazes broke out in peatland that had been drained, which made it highly {18}. Orangutans are especially {19} to such disasters because they breed so slowly. After earlier fires, researchers recorded a worrying {20} in the number of pregnancies. Scientists stress that the link is not yet proven, but the evidence is hard to {21}. Conservation groups say the {22} of injured animals is only a short-term answer. They call for the {23} of drained peatland so that it can no longer burn so easily. Without such action, the {24} of orangutans in the wild may be at risk.

items.why: An adverb is needed before the adjective “dry”, and the meaning is negative: usual → unusually.
After “highly” we need an adjective meaning “easily set on fire”: flame → flammable.
After “are especially” we need the adjective: vulnerability → vulnerable.
After “a worrying” we need a noun: “a worrying decline in the number of pregnancies.”
“Hard to dismiss” means hard to ignore or reject: miss → dismiss.
After “the” and before “of” we need a noun: rehabilitate → rehabilitation (helping injured animals recover).
After “the” and before “of” we need a noun meaning “making wet again”: wet → rewetting.
After “the” we need a noun: survive → survival.

parts.title: Key word transformation
parts.task: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between three and six words, including the word given.

items.s1: Most of the increase in sales is due to higher prices.
items.why: “Account for” means to be the reason for or to make up a part of something.

items.s1: Fewer shoppers are planning to do all their shopping on Black Friday this year.
items.post: to do all their shopping on Black Friday.
items.why: “Less likely to + verb” expresses a lower probability, matching “fewer … are planning.”

items.s1: The FCC did not block the plan, although rivals objected strongly.
items.pre: The FCC did not block the plan
items.why: “In spite of” is followed by a noun phrase and means the same as “although.”

items.s1: SpaceX must meet its deadlines; otherwise, it will lose its licence.
items.why: “Unless” means “if … not”: it will lose the licence if it does not meet the deadlines.

items.s1: The researchers could not prove that the fires caused the losses.
items.post: that the fires caused the losses.
items.why: “Be unable to + verb” is a more formal way of saying “could not.”

items.s1: It is possible that the 2026 fires did more damage than the 2015 fires.
items.why: “May have + past participle” expresses a possibility about the past.
